questions.text: "Poule mouillée" (wet chicken) really means someone is:
questions.funFact: In French, calling someone a "poule mouillée" means they're a scaredy-cat! The image is of a chicken that got rained on and looks miserable and helpless.

questions.text: What does "Haut comme trois pommes" (high as 3 apples) describe?
questions.funFact: This expression is used affectionately to describe someone very short, especially children. Three stacked apples is about 30 cm!

questions.text: If someone "tombe dans les pommes" (falls in the apples), they are:
questions.funFact: This quirky expression may come from a letter by George Sand where she wrote about being "dans les pommes cuites" (in the cooked apples) meaning exhausted.

questions.text: What does "Les doigts dans le nez" (fingers in the nose) mean?
questions.funFact: The idea is that the task is so easy you could do it with your fingers in your nose — meaning you don't even need your hands! Similar to the English "with one hand tied behind my back."

questions.text: What does "Avoir le cafard" (have the cockroach) mean?
questions.funFact: This expression was popularized by the poet Charles Baudelaire. The cockroach symbolizes the dark, gloomy feeling of melancholy crawling inside you.

questions.text: "Tiré par les cheveux" (pulled by the hair) really means something is:
questions.funFact: Just like pulling someone by the hair is a stretch, this expression means an explanation or story has been stretched too far to be believable!

questions.text: "Avoir la banane" (to have the banana) really means:
questions.funFact: The banana shape resembles a big grin! When French people say someone "has the banana," it means they have a huge smile on their face.

questions.text: "Quand les poules auront des dents" (when chickens will have teeth) really means:
questions.funFact: Since chickens will never grow teeth, this is the French equivalent of "when pigs fly!" It means something will never happen.

questions.text: "Il n'y a pas de quoi fouetter un chat" (no reason to whip a cat) really means:
choices: This is nothing to worry about
questions.funFact: This expression dates back to the 17th century. It means the situation is so minor that it's not even worth punishing a cat for — in other words, it's no big deal!

questions.text: "Avoir un poil dans la main" (to have a hair in the hand) really means:
questions.funFact: The idea is that the person is so lazy that a hair has had time to grow in the palm of their hand because they never use it for work!
